title: Becoming a parent
intro: Nothing prepares you for it: the joy, the exhaustion, the fear that you will get it wrong. The saints who raised children did it in ordinary houses, some of them in courts and some of them in prison cells. They do not offer a technique, but they show what a parent can give, whatever the age of the child: patient presence, example, and prayer.

mentors.name: Monica
mentors.why: Monica raised Augustine, who for years rejected the faith she taught him and once slipped away from her to sail for Rome. She kept praying, and a bishop she consulted told her not to lose hope.

step.label: Butler, St. Monica
step.quote: Go : contmue to do as you do ; it is impossible that a child of such tears should perish
step.note: The bishop's advice to a mother who had prayed for years over a wayward son.

mentors.name: Margaret of Scotland
mentors.why: Queen Margaret had a large family and treated their upbringing as her first duty. Butler says she chose their tutors with great care, watched over them, examined her children's progress, and often taught them herself.

step.label: Butler, St. Margaret, Queen of Scotland
step.quote: No sooner were the young princesses of an age capable of profiting by her example, than she made them her companions in her spiritual exercises and good works.
step.note: Butler stresses that she taught her children by what they saw her do.

mentors.name: Perpetua
mentors.why: Perpetua was twenty-two, married, and nursing her baby when she was arrested at Carthage. Her own account records how much the separation from her infant cost her.

step.label: Butler, SS. Perpetua and Felicitas
step.quote: I was moreover tortured with concern, for that I had not my infant.
step.note: A young mother's own words from prison. Butler records that the deacons paid for the prisoners to spend some hours in a better part of the prison, where her starving baby was brought to her and she nursed him.

title: A difficult marriage
ask: My marriage is hard, and I do not know how much more I can take.
intro: Some saints were married to people who were hot-tempered, unfaithful or careless with money, and their lives were not tidy. The Church takes marriage seriously, and it also does not ask anyone to pretend that suffering in a marriage is easy or minor. These lives show people who stayed honest and kept praying in a hard house. They are not a rule for every case. Patience is not the same as putting up with abuse: if you or your children are being hurt or are afraid, the Church does not ask you to stay in danger. She permits spouses to separate when living together becomes unsafe or practically impossible (Catechism 1649), and the spouses remain married before God. Seek safety first, then a priest, counsellor or helpline you trust.

mentors.name: Monica
mentors.why: Monica was married to Patricius, whom Butler calls good-natured and loving but hasty and choleric; Butler adds that he was unfaithful, and that it was never known that he struck her. She also had a difficult mother-in-law. Butler credits her patience, not argument in the heat of the moment, with winning both of them over in time.

step.label: Butler, St. Monica
step.quote: Monica never thwarted him by the least action or word while she saw him in anger ; but when the fit was over and he was calm, she mildly gave him her reasons
step.note: Butler on how she handled a husband's temper. He stresses that Patricius never struck her, so this is not a model for living with violence.

mentors.name: Elizabeth of Portugal
mentors.why: Her husband King Denis was unfaithful in his youth. Jealous rumour later led him to banish her from court. She kept on caring for him, and she worked to reconcile him with their rebellious son.

step.label: Butler, St. Elizabeth, Queen of Portugal
step.quote: she made it her principal study to pay to her husband the most dutiful respect, love, and obedience, and bore his injuries with invincible meekness and patience.
step.note: Butler's summary of her conduct toward a husband who wronged her.

mentors.name: Catherine of Genoa
mentors.why: Catherine was married by her father to Julian Adorno, and Butler says his temper, extravagance and ambitions caused her ten years of grief. She met it with prayer and patience, and Butler says that in the end her husband died a penitent. Her years of hospital work came afterwards.

step.label: Butler, St. Catherine of Genoa
step.quote: Her husband, drunk with youth, and giddy with ambition, brought on her a long series of grievous afflictions, which she suffered during ten years
step.note: Butler on the first years of her marriage.

title: Finding your way as a teenager
ask: I am a teenager and I do not know who I am or what I want.
intro: Being young is confusing, and the saints went through it too. Some made foolish choices, some were bullied for being serious about God, and some simply wrestled with their own character. They were not born finished.

mentors.name: Augustine of Hippo
mentors.why: At sixteen Augustine joined friends in stealing pears he did not even want. Decades later he used the memory to ask what he was really looking for.

step.label: Augustine, Confessions 2
step.quote: What then did wretched I so love in thee, thou theft of mine, thou deed of darkness, in that sixteenth year of my age?
step.note: Augustine looks back on a teenage prank as a question about desire and belonging.

mentors.name: Stanislaus Kostka
mentors.why: As a student in Vienna Stanislaus lived with an older brother who resented his piety. He was treated harshly for taking his faith seriously.

step.label: Butler, St. Stanislas Kostka
step.quote: looking upon his brother's conduct as a censure of his own, treated him continually with injuries, and often struck and beat him.
step.note: Butler on what his brother did to him at school.

mentors.name: Clare of Assisi
mentors.why: Clare came from a wealthy family and was drawn by the preaching of Francis. Butler gives the date she left home as 18 March 1212, the evening of Palm Sunday.

step.label: Butler, St. Clare
step.quote: the evening following it, being the 18th of March, 1212, she made her escape from home, accompanied with another devout young woman, and went a mile out of the town to the Portiuncula, where St. Francis lived with his little community.
step.note: A young woman's decisive night, described by Butler.

mentors.name: Thérèse of Lisieux
mentors.why: As a girl Thérèse was so sensitive that tears came easily. She felt stuck, until what she calls a turning on Christmas Day 1886, when she was thirteen.

step.label: Thérèse, Story of a Soul
step.quote: My extreme sensitiveness made me almost unbearable. All arguments were useless. I simply could not correct myself of this miserable fault.
step.note: Her honest description of her own temperament in the years before Christmas 1886.

title: Choosing a vocation
ask: What am I supposed to do with my life?
intro: Marriage, priesthood, religious life, single life, a trade or a profession: the question is real and the saints asked it too. Some got an answer slowly and some got a surprising one. Their writings ask for honest intentions more than for a sign from heaven.

mentors.name: Ignatius of Loyola
mentors.why: Ignatius was a wounded soldier who wanted romances to read in bed. They only had lives of Christ and the saints, and that reading began to change him. He later wrote guidance for making life decisions.

step.label: Ignatius, Spiritual Exercises
step.quote: In every good election, as far as depends on us, the eye of our intention ought to be simple, only looking at what we are created for, namely, the praise of God our Lord and the salvation of our soul.
step.note: Ignatius's test for any big choice is where it leads, not whether it is exciting.

mentors.name: Francis de Sales
mentors.why: As bishop Francis wrote for lay people and insisted that holiness is not reserved for monasteries.

step.label: Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life
step.quote: It is an error, nay more, a very heresy, to seek to banish the devout life from the soldier’s guardroom, the mechanic’s workshop, the prince’s court, or the domestic hearth.
step.note: A reminder that an ordinary calling can be a path to God.

mentors.name: Thérèse of Lisieux
mentors.why: Thérèse felt drawn to be a missionary, a priest, a martyr and a teacher all at once, and could not see how one life could hold them. She writes that she found her place by reading 1 Corinthians 12-13 and reflecting on love.

step.label: Thérèse, Story of a Soul
step.quote: O Jesus, my Love, at last I have found my vocation. My vocation is love!
step.note: Her own account of the moment her questions settled.

mentors.name: Francis of Assisi
mentors.why: Before his calling was clear, Francis was drawn toward the poor and the sick. Butler's account of his meeting with a leper is a turning point in his story.

step.label: Butler, St. Francis of Assisi
step.quote: Riding one day in the plains of Assisium, he met a leper whose sores were so loathsome, that at the sight of them he was struck with horror, and suddenly recoiled ; but overcoming himself he alighted
step.note: He did something that frightened him, and that began to change his direction.

title: Starting over after a big mistake
ask: I made a terrible mistake and I do not know how to begin again.
intro: The Church has always honoured people who changed course. Gamblers, soldiers and people who wasted years became saints. They did not erase what they had done, but they began again and let God use the rest of their lives.

mentors.name: Camillus de Lellis
mentors.why: Camillus was a soldier addicted to cards, to the point of losing necessities. After a Capuchin's exhortation, he repented, and he eventually founded an order to care for the sick.

step.label: Butler, St. Camillus de Lellis
step.quote: He had contracted so violent a passion for cards and gaming, that he sometimes lost even necessaries.
step.note: Butler is frank about the habit he had to overcome.

mentors.name: Margaret of Cortona
mentors.why: Margaret lived in grave sin, then repented. Butler says she went first to her father, then to public penance, and spent the rest of her life as a penitent.

step.label: Butler, St. Margaret of Cortona
step.quote: The first thing she did was to throw herself at her father's feet, bathed in tears, to beg his pardon for her contempt of his authority and fatherly admonitions.
step.note: Her first step was to face the person she had hurt.

mentors.name: Augustine of Hippo
mentors.why: Augustine spent years in ambition, an unwed relationship and false teachings before he gave himself to God. He later wrote about how late it came.

step.label: Augustine, Confessions 10
step.quote: Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee!
step.note: Regret and gratitude together, written years after his conversion.

mentors.name: Peter the Apostle
mentors.why: Peter had promised he would never abandon Jesus, and then denied that he knew him three times in one night. Luke records the look Jesus gave him, and what Peter did next. Later accounts show him forgiven and given work to do.

step.label: Luke 22:60-62
step.quote: He went out, and wept bitterly.
step.note: Peter did not excuse himself; he faced what he had done.

title: Ambition and pride
ask: I want to get ahead, and I worry that I am proud.
intro: Wanting to do well is not a sin, but the saints noticed how easily it turns into wanting to be admired. Several of them held real power, and their stories show what it takes to hold it lightly.

mentors.name: Augustine of Hippo
mentors.why: As a professor of rhetoric in Milan, Augustine was about to give a speech praising the emperor. He admits he knew it would include lies, and he saw a cheerful beggar on the street.

step.label: Augustine, Confessions 6
step.quote: I was preparing to recite a panegyric of the Emperor, wherein I was to utter many a lie, and lying, was to be applauded by those who knew I lied
step.note: His honest account of what career success was costing him.

mentors.name: Francis Borgia
mentors.why: Borgia was a duke and a favourite at the court of Charles V. When he had to take oath that the disfigured body of the dead empress was hers, he began to ask what he was chasing.

step.label: Butler, St. Francis Borgia
step.quote: How long shall I pursue and grasp at shadows
step.note: Butler records his prayer after seeing the empress's coffin.

mentors.name: Gregory the Great
mentors.why: Gregory had left a public career for a monastery. When he was elected pope he tried to avoid it, even leaving Rome in a basket, and was found and consecrated.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory the Great
step.quote: he prevailed with certain merchants to carry him off disguised, and shut up in a wicker basket.
step.note: Gregory's attempt to flee the papacy.

title: Having money and wanting to give
ask: I have more than I need and I am not sure what to do with it.
intro: Money is not condemned in the saints' lives, but they treated it as something held for others. Some gave away everything, others kept their duties as rulers and gave from what they had. Their stories are honest that generosity can cost friendships.

mentors.name: Paulinus of Nola
mentors.why: Paulinus was a senator, a consul, and married to a rich wife. He sold his estates for the poor, and Butler records that his own family turned against him.

step.label: Butler, St. Paulinus of Nola
step.quote: The saint sold all his estates, and distributed the price among the poor
step.note: Butler adds that relatives and former friends rejected him for it.

mentors.name: Antony the Abbot
mentors.why: Antony inherited land when about twenty, and one Sunday heard the story of the rich young man. He took it as spoken to him.

step.label: Butler, St. Antony, Abbot
step.quote: He considered these words as addressed to himself; going home, he made over to his neighbors three hundred aruras
step.note: He gave away the land, kept enough for his sister, and began a new life.

mentors.name: Paula
mentors.why: A Roman noblewoman, Paula spent her money on the needy. Butler says she regarded it as a loss if anyone else gave help in her place.

step.label: Butler, St. Paula
step.quote: gave every thing to the poor which it was in her power to dispose of. She was careful in inquiring after the necessitous, and deemed it a loss on her side if any other hands than her own administered relief to them.
step.note: She sought out the people who needed help.

mentors.name: Louis IX of France
mentors.why: King Louis ran a kingdom and an army. Butler stresses that he lived simply and served the poor in person.

step.label: Butler, St. Lewis, King of France
step.quote: more particularly towards the poor, often serving them at table, washing their feet, and visiting them in the hospitals.
step.note: A man with power who chose to do the lowest service himself.

title: Poverty and need
ask: I am struggling to make ends meet.
intro: The saints do not say that being poor is good in itself. Several of them were poor, hungry or driven out of their homes, and they found work to do, and a way to pray, without pretending that it was easy.

mentors.name: Isidore the Farmer
mentors.why: Isidore was a day labourer in Madrid, born to poor parents who could not afford schooling for him.

step.label: Butler, St. Isidore of Madrid
step.quote: He was born at Madrid, of poor but very devout parents, and was christened Isidore from the name of their patron, St. Isidore of Seville.
step.note: Butler stresses that his poverty did not keep him from a rich prayer life.

mentors.name: Elizabeth of Hungary
mentors.why: A princess who fed hundreds each day, Elizabeth was driven out of her castle after her husband died. She and her children had to beg shelter.

step.label: Butler, St. Elizabeth of Hungary
step.quote: Thus she, who had entertained thousands of poor, could find no entertainment or harbor
step.note: Butler on the winter she lost everything.

mentors.name: John of God
mentors.why: After a dramatic conversion in Granada, John began selling wood in the market to feed poor people, and then opened a house for the sick.

step.label: Butler, St. John of God
step.quote: he began by selling wood in the market-place, to feed some poor by the means of his labor.
step.note: He started with what he had, a day's labour.

title: Imprisonment or persecution
ask: I am being held, silenced or persecuted.
intro: Many saints were chained, exiled or killed for their faith. Their accounts are honest about fear, hunger and cold, and also about a quiet hope that did not depend on being freed.

mentors.name: Perpetua
mentors.why: Perpetua was twenty-two and a new mother when she was imprisoned in Carthage. The prison account that bears her name is among the earliest writings attributed to a Christian woman.

step.label: Butler, SS. Perpetua and Felicitas
step.quote: I was shocked at the horror and darkness of the place; for till then I knew not what such sort of places were.
step.note: Her first reaction to the cell, in her own words.

mentors.name: Ignatius of Antioch
mentors.why: Ignatius was condemned in Antioch and taken in chains to Rome. According to Butler, he thanked God for the chains.

step.label: Butler, St. Ignatius of Antioch
step.quote: I thank thee, O Lord, for vouchsafing to honor me with this token of perfect love for thee, and to be bound with chains of iron, in imitation of thy apostle Paul, for thy sake.
step.note: His words on hearing the sentence.

mentors.name: Martin I
mentors.why: Pope Martin was arrested by the emperor, mistreated, and exiled to the Crimea, where there was famine.

step.label: Butler, St. Martin I
step.quote: St. Martin was more afflicted at the injuries which his benefactors received than at his own sufferings.
step.note: He worried about the people who had been kind to him.

mentors.name: Vincent de Paul
mentors.why: According to a traditional account that Butler repeats, Vincent was captured by pirates and sold as a slave in Tunis. He later spent his life serving the poor.

step.label: Butler, St. Vincent de Paul
step.quote: Then they gave to every slave a pair of loose breeches, a linen jerkin, and a bonnet. In this garb they were led five or six times through the city of Tunis to be shown
step.note: Butler on what the slave market was like.

title: War and violence around you
ask: There is violence near me and I do not know what a Christian should do.
intro: If you or someone near you is in danger, get to safety and call for help first. These stories are about soldiers and rulers; they are not a call to take up arms. The saints answered war differently: some refused to fight, some fought and tried to limit it, and some tried to stop it by talking. Their stories do not agree on every point, but all of them refused to treat violence as normal. The Catechism asks everyone to work to avoid war, allows lawful defence only under strict conditions, honours soldiers who serve honourably, and asks public authorities to make fair provision for those who refuse to bear arms for reasons of conscience (Catechism 2308-2311).

mentors.name: Martin of Tours
mentors.why: Martin was a Roman soldier who asked for discharge before a battle. Butler says he offered to stand unarmed in front of the troops instead of fighting.

step.label: Butler, St. Martin of Tours
step.quote: He therefore begged that his donative might be bestowed on some other person, and asked his dismission, that he might give himself up totally to the service of Christ.
step.note: He chose to leave the army.

mentors.name: Maximilian of Tebessa
mentors.why: Maximilian was the son of a soldier. Called up at twenty-one, he refused the mark of army service (a print on the band and a leaden collar bearing the emperor's name) and was beheaded. Butler gives his reason as the pagan practices of the army; the early account of his trial is usually read as having him say that he could not serve as a soldier, because he was a Christian. His choice cost him his life and is not a rule for every Christian.

step.label: Butler, St. Maximilian
step.quote: His plea was, that in the Roman army superstitions, contrary to the Christian faith, were often practised, with which he could not defile his soul.
step.note: A young man who accepted death rather than serve.

mentors.name: Leo the Great
mentors.why: When Attila marched toward Rome, the city sent Pope Leo to meet him. Butler says Attila received him honourably and agreed to a treaty.

step.label: Butler, St. Leo the Great
step.quote: in hopes of mollifying his rage, and averting the danger that threatened his country.
step.note: A bishop went unarmed to face an invader.

mentors.name: Augustine of Hippo
mentors.why: Augustine wrote to a Roman general about how to conduct himself in war.

step.label: Augustine, Letter 189
step.quote: Peace should be the object of your desire; war should be waged only as a necessity, and waged only that God may by it deliver men from the necessity and preserve them in peace.
step.note: Augustine, writing to a Roman general, says war may be waged only out of necessity and for the sake of peace. He does not treat it as a good.

title: Being a stranger in a new land
ask: I live in a place that is not my own.
intro: Many saints were far from home, by capture, by calling, or by choice. They knew loneliness, strange languages and suspicion, and some of them also became important to the places that received them.

mentors.name: Patrick
mentors.why: At sixteen Patrick was captured and taken to Ireland, where he herded cattle. He later returned there as a bishop.

step.label: Butler, St. Patrick
step.quote: They took him into Ireland, where he was obliged to keep cattle on the mountains and in the forests, in hunger and nakedness, amidst snows, rain, and ice.
step.note: Butler on his years as a slave.

mentors.name: Vincent de Paul
mentors.why: Vincent was sold as a slave in Tunis, far from France. Butler describes how he and the other captives were paraded and examined.

step.label: Butler, St. Vincent de Paul
step.quote: as men do at the sale of a horse or an ox. They examined who could eat well, felt their sides, looked at their teeth
step.note: His first days in a foreign land were humiliating.

mentors.name: Columban
mentors.why: Columban left Ireland with twelve companions and settled in Gaul. Butler reports that they were noticed for their gentleness.

step.label: Butler, St. Columban
step.quote: He was so humble that he always contended with his twelve companions for the lowest place.
step.note: Strangers in a new land, living simply and drawing admiration at first.

mentors.name: Paula
mentors.why: Paula left Rome, her home, and moved to Bethlehem. Butler quotes her words on first seeing the manger.

step.label: Butler, St. Paula
step.quote: I, a miserable sinner, am made worthy to kiss the manger, in which my Lord was pleased to be laid an infant babe weeping for me!
step.note: She found her home in a foreign city.

title: Old age and being forgotten
ask: I am getting old, and I feel like nobody needs me.
intro: Age brings loss of strength, loss of work, and sometimes loss of attention. The saints who lived long did not pretend otherwise. They kept doing what they could and kept praying.

mentors.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
mentors.why: Polycarp was a very old man when the proconsul urged him to deny Christ. He spoke of his long years of service.

step.label: Butler, St. Polycarp
step.quote: I have served him these fourscore and six years, and he never did me any harm, but much good
step.note: A lifetime of faith, summed up in one sentence.

mentors.name: Bede
mentors.why: Bede, in his last days, kept dictating an English translation of John's Gospel to his students. Butler quotes him as saying he would not have his scholars read a falsehood after his death.

step.label: Butler, St. Bede
step.quote: Go on quickly ; I know not how long I shall hold out, and whether my Maker will soon take me away.
step.note: He worked up to the end, calmly.

mentors.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
mentors.why: After years of church politics and slander, and in poor health, Gregory retired to the family estate near Arianzum. Butler calls him very old and infirm, though by the usual dates he was in his fifties; the point is that he was sick and out of public life, yet still advised the local church.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: spent the remainder of his life in retirement near Arianzum ; still continuing to aid that church with his advice, though at that time very old and infirm.
step.note: He found a quieter way to be useful.

title: A hard boss or a job you dislike
ask: My boss is difficult and I dread going to work.
intro: Most holy men and women did ordinary work. Some had cruel employers, some had jobs they did not like, and they did not find an easy answer, but each found a way to do the work without losing their peace. If your work is unsafe or abusive, seek help and consider leaving.

mentors.name: Brother Lawrence
mentors.why: Lawrence was a cook in a monastery. He did not like the kitchen, and by his own account he learned to do his work as an offering. His story is about a job he disliked, not a difficult boss.

step.label: Brother Lawrence, Practice of the Presence of God
step.quote: So, likewise, in his business in the kitchen (to which he had naturally a great aversion), having accustomed himself to do everything there for the love of God, and with prayer, upon all occasions, for His grace to do his work well, he had found everything easy, during the fifteen years that he had been employed there.
step.note: A hated job became bearable when he changed what it was for.

mentors.name: Zita
mentors.why: Zita was a household servant in Lucca. For years the family and other servants misjudged and mistreated her, and Butler says she was often beaten, which no worker should be asked to accept. Her story is about the peace of her heart, not a rule that abuse must be endured. She kept serving faithfully, and in time they came to trust her.

step.label: Butler, St. Zita
step.quote: So unjustly despised, overburdened, reviled, and often beaten, she never repined nor lost her patience
step.note: Butler on her early years in service.

mentors.name: Isidore the Farmer
mentors.why: Isidore was a farm labourer who faced the envy of other workers. Butler says he answered it with kindness.

step.label: Butler, St. Isidore of Madrid
step.quote: His patience in bearing all injuries and in overcoming the envy of fellow-servants by cordial kindnesses
step.note: Butler's summary of how he handled workplace resentment.

title: Wanting to be closer to God
ask: I want to pray and I do not know how to start.
intro: The holy men and women who wrote about prayer were beginners too. Several admit they gave it up at times. Their advice is simple: keep at it, trust God, and do not wait until you feel ready.

mentors.name: Augustine of Hippo
mentors.why: Augustine is known for a sentence he wrote at the start of the Confessions.

step.label: Augustine, Confessions 1
step.quote: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
step.note: The desire for God is part of being human.

mentors.name: Teresa of Avila
mentors.why: Teresa stopped praying for a time because she felt unworthy, and she later said that was a mistake.

step.label: Teresa of Avila, Life
step.quote: let him never cease from prayer who has once begun it, be his life ever so wicked; for prayer is the way to amend it, and without prayer such amendment will be much more difficult.
step.note: Her advice, from her own failure, not to give up.

mentors.name: Brother Lawrence
mentors.why: Lawrence taught that prayer can be a habit of remembering God in the middle of daily work.

step.label: Brother Lawrence, Practice of the Presence of God
step.quote: Were I a preacher, I should above all other things preach the practice of the presence of God; and were I a director, I should advise all the world to do it: so necessary do I think it, and so easy too.
step.note: A simple practice open to anyone.

mentors.name: Julian of Norwich
mentors.why: Julian, an anchoress in Norwich, wrote about prayer after a series of visions.

step.label: Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love
step.quote: Then saw I truly that it is more worship to God, and more very delight, that we faithfully pray to Himself of His Goodness and cleave thereunto by His Grace, with true understanding, and steadfast by love, than if we took all the means that heart can think.
step.note: Prayer does not need to be elaborate.
